lesson.intro: A coding interview is not a test of whether you have seen the problem before. It is a short work sample: can you take a fuzzy problem, make it precise, solve it and convince someone your code is right, while working like a teammate. This lesson walks through the whole process from application to offer, how to handle online assessments and their rules, a method you can run on any problem, and a plan to practice until it is automatic.
objectives: Describe each stage from application to offer and what it tests
Handle an online assessment: rules, constraints, partial credit and the clock
Apply a six-step method (understand, match, plan, implement, review, evaluate) to a new problem
Think out loud and test your own code by hand in a way that earns credit
Plan weekly practice with spaced re-solving, timed sets and mock interviews

sections.title: The process: from application to offer
sections.body:
Picture September of your third year. You apply to 40 internships. A week later an email arrives: "Complete this online assessment within 7 days." Two weeks after that a recruiter wants a 20-minute call, then an engineer schedules a 45-minute technical interview, and finally you are invited to a "final round." Each stage filters for something different, so it pays to know which one you are in.

- **Application review.** A recruiter, sometimes helped by filters on the application form, decides whether you get the next step. Your resume does the work here.
- **Online assessment (OA).** A timed coding test scored automatically by hidden test cases. The next section covers it in detail.
- **Recruiter screen.** 15 to 30 minutes about your background, interests, graduation date, location and logistics. Mostly behavioral: have your one-minute "tell me about yourself" ready and know why you want the role.
- **Technical phone screen.** About 45 to 60 minutes with an engineer in a shared editor, usually one or two problems. Often you cannot run the code, so your explanation and your hand testing carry the weight.
- **Final round (the onsite or virtual loop).** Two to five back-to-back interviews, now often over video. For interns it is commonly two technical interviews plus a behavioral one, sometimes with a hiring manager. Each interviewer usually writes feedback independently, and the decision looks at the whole set, sometimes in a hiring committee.
- **Team matching,** at some large companies. After you pass, you may talk with a few managers who are choosing interns. These are short conversations about your interests and their work; treat them as interviews in both directions.
- **Offer.** Usually a call from the recruiter, then a written offer with a deadline. The internship search pack covers what to do next.

The order varies (some companies put the recruiter screen before the OA), and the whole process can take anywhere from a couple of weeks to a couple of months. Silence of a week or two between stages is normal. If the date the recruiter gave you has passed, one short, polite email asking for an update is fine.

Smaller companies and startups vary more. Some skip the OA and use a take-home project, a pair-programming session on a real codebase, or a conversation about a project you built. The core skills are the same everywhere: solve the problem, communicate while you do it, and verify your work.
sections.code:
Stage            Length       Graded by     Mostly tests
OA               60-120 min   hidden tests  correct code,
                                            edge cases
Recruiter        15-30 min    recruiter     interest, fit,
                                            logistics
Phone screen     45-60 min    one engineer  solve, explain,
                                            test
Final loop       2-5 x 45 min several       the same, plus
                              people        behavioral
sections.tip: Ask the recruiter what each round looks like. They want you to succeed and will usually tell you the format, the length and whether you can run code.
sections.pitfall: Treating every stage the same. A recruiter screen needs a crisp story about you, an OA needs correct code fast, and a phone screen needs you to talk while you solve.

check.question: Two weeks after a phone screen, you have heard nothing, and the recruiter said to expect news "within a week". What is the best move?
choices: Assume you were rejected and stop preparing
Email the interviewer directly and ask how you did
Send the recruiter one short, polite note asking whether there is an update on next steps
Apply again to the same role so your name comes up
check.explanation: Delays are common and usually mean scheduling or internal reviews, not a decision. One polite note to the recruiter, who owns the process, is normal. Interviewers usually cannot share results, and reapplying adds noise.

sections.title: Online assessments: format, rules and the clock
sections.body:
An online assessment, or OA, is often the first technical filter, and at many large internship programs it is the step that removes the most applicants. It is a timed test on a platform such as HackerRank, CodeSignal or Codility, or on the company's own tool. Formats vary, but the common pieces are:

- **Coding problems:** typically one to four problems in roughly 60 to 120 minutes, often an easier one plus one or two medium ones. Your code runs against test cases, many of them hidden, and you usually get credit for each test that passes.
- **Other sections** some companies add: multiple-choice questions on complexity or output, a broken function to debug, a work-style survey, or a work simulation where you answer messages and make decisions as if you already had the job.
- **A window to start in:** you often get several days to begin, and once you press Start the timer runs without pausing.

**Rules and proctoring.** Read the instructions page every time; it is not the same everywhere. Some OAs record your screen, webcam or browser activity, and many flag pasted code and switching away from the test tab. Treat AI assistants, solution websites and help from other people as forbidden unless the rules explicitly allow them: platforms run similarity checks across submissions, and a cheating flag can bar you from that company. Whether you may open language documentation also varies, so check. Pick a quiet place, a reliable connection and a charged laptop, and use the practice test most platforms offer to learn the editor before the real one.

**Time management** is where most points are lost:

- **Read every problem first,** about a minute each, noting the constraints. Start with the one you are surest of.
- **Get a correct solution before a fast one.** A brute force that passes the small tests earns partial credit. Then let the constraints tell you how fast it must be: with n up to 100,000, an O(n^2) loop will usually time out, while O(n log n) is comfortable. Tiny limits such as n up to 20 hint that an exponential search is acceptable.
- **Test edge cases before submitting:** empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives and the maximum size. Hidden tests almost always include them.
- **Watch the clock.** If one problem has eaten half your time with nothing passing, submit what you have and move on.
- **Use the language you know best,** with standard library tools you can write from memory.

**How to practice:** do timed sets, not only untimed puzzles. Once you know a few patterns, sit two or three challenges from the challenge bank against a 70-minute timer with no hints, then review every miss. The activity shows why constraints matter so much.
sections.tip: Write down the start time and a halfway checkpoint on paper. Without one, it is easy to look up and find 15 minutes left on a problem you have not started.
sections.pitfall: Spending the whole OA perfecting the first problem. Each problem usually counts separately, so a working brute force on every problem often scores more than one perfect solution.

activity.title: Read the constraints
activity.prompt: A common rule of thumb is that a typical time limit fits around 10^8 simple steps in a fast language, and noticeably fewer in Python. Run it to see which complexities fit for each input size. Then add n = 20 and an "O(2^n)" row and notice why tiny limits invite brute-force search.

props.task: Add 20 to the list of sizes and an ("O(2^n)", 2 ** n) row, then run it again.

check.question: An OA problem says n can be as large as 200,000. Your nested-loop solution passes the small sample. What should you expect?
choices: It will pass every hidden test, because the sample passed
Hidden tests with large n will likely time out, so look for an O(n log n) or O(n) approach
The platform will automatically speed up nested loops
Large inputs are never tested in OAs
check.explanation: At n = 200,000 an O(n^2) loop is about 4 x 10^10 steps, far beyond what a time limit allows. Samples are small on purpose; the hidden tests check the stated limits, so the constraints tell you the complexity you need.

sections.title: A method you can run on any problem
sections.body:
A typical phone-screen prompt: "Given a string, return the first character that does not repeat. If there is none, return an empty string." Strong candidates do not start typing. They run the same six steps every time, a method often called **UMPIRE**:

- **Understand.** Restate the problem in your own words. Write two or three examples, including edge cases, and ask about anything unclear: "Is it case-sensitive? Can the string be empty? Only lowercase letters, or any character?"
- **Match.** Ask which known pattern fits. Counting things and looking them up quickly points to a hash map.
- **Plan.** Describe the approach in plain words or pseudocode and state its expected complexity. Get a nod from the interviewer before writing code.
- **Implement.** Write clean code with clear names. Keep talking, but about decisions, not keystrokes.
- **Review.** Trace your code on an example, line by line, and run the edge cases you listed.
- **Evaluate.** State the time and space complexity and mention trade-offs or possible improvements.

Applied to the prompt: the examples are `"leetcode"` gives `"l"`, `"loveleetcode"` gives `"v"`, `"aabb"` gives `""`, and the empty string gives `""`. The pattern is counting with a hash map. The plan is two passes: count every character, then scan the string again and return the first character whose count is 1. Each pass is O(n), so the whole thing is O(n) time.

**Which language?** Use the one you are most fluent in. Python is popular because it is short to write, but fluency matters more than the language: you should be able to use its dictionary, set, sorting with a key, a queue and a heap without looking anything up, so your attention stays on the problem.
sections.tip: Type your examples into the editor as comments. They become your test cases in the Review step, and the interviewer can see your thinking.
sections.pitfall: Skipping Understand to save time. Many failed interviews go wrong in the first five minutes: a missed constraint or a wrong assumption makes everything after it wasted work.

check.question: You have restated the problem and written examples. What should happen before you write any code?
choices: Start coding the brute force right away so you have something
Explain your planned approach and its complexity, and check the interviewer agrees
Ask the interviewer which data structure they expect you to use
Set up a full unit-testing framework in the editor
check.explanation: Plan comes before Implement. Saying the approach and its complexity out loud lets the interviewer redirect you before you spend 15 minutes coding the wrong idea. Asking which data structure they expect hands them the problem solving you are being scored on.

sections.title: Thinking out loud, and how you are scored
sections.body:
Two candidates solve the same problem with the same final code. One gets a strong hire, the other a no hire. The difference is almost always what the interviewer could see and hear along the way.

Most companies score coding interviews on some version of four areas:

- **Problem solving.** Did you understand the problem, find a reasonable approach and improve it? Did you use hints well?
- **Coding.** Is the code correct, readable and idiomatic? Good names, small helpers, no tangled conditions.
- **Communication.** Could the interviewer follow your reasoning the whole time? Did you ask good questions and explain trade-offs?
- **Testing and verification.** Did you check your own code, find your own bugs and think of edge cases without being asked?

Thinking out loud is what makes problem solving, communication and testing visible. Narrate decisions and reasons, not keystrokes. When you need quiet time, say so: "Give me a minute to think about duplicates." A short, announced pause is fine. Long unexplained silence is not, because the interviewer cannot give you credit, or a hint, for thinking they cannot see.

Treat the interviewer as a teammate, not an examiner. Ask "Does that approach sound reasonable before I code it?" If they push back, they are usually trying to help you.
sections.code:
WEAK    "OK, for loop... i... range... n."
STRONG  "I'll loop once and keep a set of values I've
         seen, so each check is O(1)."

WEAK    (four minutes of silence)
STRONG  "I'm stuck on duplicates. Let me try a tiny
         example: [2, 2, 3]."

WEAK    "Done. I think it works."
STRONG  "Before I call it done, let me trace [2, 7, 11]
         with target 9."
sections.tip: Practice thinking out loud alone first: solve a problem while recording yourself, then listen back. It feels awkward for a week, then it becomes normal.
sections.pitfall: Going quiet when things get hard. That is exactly when narration helps most, because it lets the interviewer see where you are and nudge you.

check.question: A candidate writes correct, clean code in silence, then says "done" without testing it. Which two scoring areas are most likely to suffer?
choices: Coding and problem solving
Problem solving and testing
Coding and communication
Communication and testing
check.explanation: The code was correct and clean, so coding is fine, and reaching a working solution shows problem solving. Silence hurts communication, and declaring it done without checking hurts testing and verification.

sections.title: When you are stuck
sections.body:
Fifteen minutes in, you have a brute-force idea and nothing better. Everyone gets here, including people who get offers. What separates them is having moves to make instead of freezing.

- **Say the brute force and its cost.** "Checking every pair works and is O(n^2). Let me see if I can avoid the inner loop." This proves you can solve it and gives you a baseline to improve.
- **Find the repeated work.** Work a small example by hand and watch for the moment you recompute something. Repeated lookups suggest a hash map; repeated sums suggest a running total or prefix sums.
- **Walk the pattern list.** Ask whether each common pattern could apply. The table below lists the signals to listen for.
- **Change the problem.** What if the input were sorted? What if there were only two elements? Solve the smaller or easier version first, then extend it.
- **Use hints well.** Interviewers expect to give hints. Repeat the hint in your own words and follow it. Ignoring a hint, or arguing with it, is one of the clearest negative signals.
- **Protect your time.** If ten minutes remain and you have nothing better, say so and write clean brute-force code. Working code plus a clear note on how you would optimize beats an unfinished clever idea.
sections.code:
Signal in the problem               Try first
"sorted array", "find a target"     binary search,
                                    two pointers
"contiguous subarray", "substring"  sliding window,
                                    prefix sums
"seen before?", "pair that sums"    hash map or set
"matching brackets", "next greater" stack
"top k", "kth largest"              heap
"fewest steps", grid, unweighted    breadth-first search
"all combinations", "permutations"  backtracking
"number of ways", "min cost"        dynamic programming
sections.tip: Keep the brute force as a one-line comment in the editor. If time runs out, you can point to it and to the optimization you were working toward.
sections.pitfall: Silently testing ideas in your head for five minutes. Say each idea and why it fails; the interviewer can only hint toward a path they can see you on.

check.question: You need the longest substring with no repeated characters. Which signal and pattern match best?
choices: Sorted input, so binary search
Fewest steps, so breadth-first search
All combinations, so backtracking
Contiguous substring, so sliding window
check.explanation: "Substring" means a contiguous range, and "longest with a condition" is the classic sliding-window signal: grow the right edge, shrink the left edge when a character repeats. Backtracking would explore every subset, which is exponential and unnecessary.

sections.title: Testing your own code by hand
sections.body:
You finish coding and the interviewer asks, "How do you know it works?" The weak answer is "I think it's right." The strong answer is to show it, in about three minutes, without running anything.

- **Trace one normal example.** Pick a small input and walk through the code line by line, writing down each variable's value. Read the code you actually wrote, not the code you meant to write.
- **Run the edge cases.** For most array and string problems: empty input, one element, two elements, all the same value, duplicates, negatives or zero, already sorted and reverse sorted, and the largest sizes the constraints allow.
- **Check the boundaries.** Off-by-one errors hide in loop bounds (`range(n)` versus `range(n - 1)`), in `<` versus `<=`, and in where a `return` sits.
- **Fix and re-trace.** When you find a bug, say so calmly, fix it and re-run the case that exposed it. Finding your own bug is a positive signal, not a failure.

Below is a trace of `first_unique_char("aabc")` written the way you would type it into a shared editor. In the activity, a function passes both of its "normal" tests and is still broken. Only the edge cases catch it.

activity.title: Find the bug the happy path hides
activity.prompt: Before you press Run, trace the six test cases by hand and predict which ones fail. Notice that both "normal" cases pass even though the function is broken. Then fix the bug so the output is exactly: 6 of 6 tests pass

props.task: Fix is_sorted so that every test passes.

sections.tip: List your edge cases out loud before you trace them. Even if time runs out before you check them all, the interviewer hears that you know what to test.
sections.pitfall: Tracing the code you meant to write instead of the code on the screen. Point at each line as you go, as if you were the computer.

check.question: Your function returns the largest number in a list and starts with `best = 0`. Which test case exposes a bug?
check.explanation: With only negative numbers, nothing beats the starting value 0, so the function returns 0, which is not even in the list. Start with `best = nums[0]` (after handling an empty list) instead. The other inputs all contain a positive number, so they hide the bug.

sections.title: Talking about complexity and trade-offs
sections.body:
Almost every interview ends with "What's the time and space complexity?" and often "Can you do better?" Answer like an engineer: say what n is, give both time and space, and explain where the cost comes from.

Take a classic: does a list contain a duplicate? There are three reasonable solutions, and the trade-off between them is the conversation the interviewer wants to have. A strong answer sounds like this: "With a set it's O(n) time on average and O(n) extra space, where n is the length of the list. If memory were tight and I'm allowed to modify the input, I'd sort in place and compare neighbors: O(n log n) time and little extra memory."

Habits that earn credit:

- **Define n.** For a text and a pattern, say "n is the text length and m is the pattern length." For a grid, it is rows times columns.
- **Give time and space.** Count any new list you build, and the call stack for recursion (recursion depth d costs O(d) space).
- **Say average versus worst case where it matters.** Hash map operations are O(1) on average but degrade with many collisions; quicksort is O(n log n) on average and O(n^2) in the worst case.
- **Tie trade-offs to the situation.** Faster but more memory, simpler but slower, or preprocessing that only pays off when there are many queries. There is rarely one right answer, only a right answer for the constraints you were given.
sections.code:
Contains duplicate?
                     Time          Extra space
Every pair           O(n^2)        O(1)
Sort, check pairs    O(n log n)    O(1)*
Hash set of seen     O(n) average  O(n)

* when sorting in place is allowed (Python's sort
  may still use up to O(n) internally)

activity.title: Feel the gap between growth rates
activity.prompt: Drag n up toward 1,000 and compare O(n log n) with O(n^2), then rank all the curves. When an interviewer asks "can you do better?", this gap is what they mean.

sections.pitfall: Giving only the time complexity. Interviewers almost always want space too, and forgetting a hash map's O(n) memory makes it look like you missed the trade-off.

check.question: Your solution sorts the input with Python's sorted() and then scans it once. What is the time complexity?
choices: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
check.explanation: Sorting costs O(n log n) and the scan costs O(n). The larger term dominates, so the total is O(n log n). It is not O(n), because the sort is not free.

sections.title: A practice plan, and the day itself
sections.body:
Most people prepare by grinding random problems, forget the early ones, and freeze when an interview problem doesn't look like anything they've seen. A better plan uses the same science as the rest of Recurse: learn one pattern at a time, retrieve it on a schedule, then mix everything together.

A weekly loop for 8 to 10 weeks:

- **Learn one pattern.** Do the lesson for one pattern pack (hash maps, two pointers, sliding window and so on). Recurse schedules its questions so the recognition signals and complexities come back right before you would forget them.
- **Solve 3 to 5 challenges for that pattern** from the challenge bank, out loud and with a timer. Give yourself about 25 minutes before you open a hint, and use the hints in order.
- **Re-solve, don't reread.** When you needed the solution, write one line about what you missed ("didn't see that sorted input meant two pointers"). Solve it again from a blank editor two or three days later, and again about a week after that.
- **Keep the daily review.** Ten to fifteen minutes of Recurse review a day keeps old patterns alive while you learn new ones.
- **Mix it up from week 4.** Do mixed sets where you don't know the pattern in advance, because a real interview never tells you. Choosing the pattern is a separate skill that needs its own practice.
- **Mock interviews from week 4.** Once a week, 45 minutes with a friend, a classmate or a mock interview service, with the other person choosing the problem. Swap roles too: playing the interviewer shows you what they notice.

A smaller set of problems you can re-solve from scratch and explain beats a huge pile you skimmed once. Log every attempt and let your misses drive the schedule.

**The day itself.** The day before a video interview, test the link, your camera, microphone and internet, and charge everything. Have water, paper and a pen, and turn off notifications. At the start, ask which language you may use and whether the code will run. Leave the last five minutes for your own questions. Between interviews in a loop, take a breath and reset: each interviewer starts with a blank page. Afterward, write down every problem and how it went while it is fresh, and add the misses to your practice log.
sections.code:
Date  Problem          Pattern   Time  Result
Mon   Two Sum          hash map  14m   solved
Mon   Valid Anagram    hash map  22m   hint 1
      missed: compare counts, not sorted copies
      retry: Thu
Tue   Longest Substr.  window    25m+  solution
      missed: shrink the left edge on a repeat

activity.title: Run the whole method on Two Sum
activity.prompt: Treat this as a mini interview. Start a timer, type two examples and one edge case as comments, say the brute force and its complexity out loud, then code the hash map version and trace one example by hand before you run the tests. Log your time and anything you missed, and re-solve it from a blank editor in three days.

sections.tip: Book your first mock interviews before you feel ready. The first two usually feel rough, and you want that to happen in practice, not in a real loop.
sections.pitfall: Reading a solution, nodding and moving on. Recognizing a solution is much easier than producing one; only re-solving from a blank editor tells you whether you have learned it.

check.question: You opened the solution for a sliding-window problem after 25 minutes. What is the most effective next step?
choices: Mark it done and move on to a new problem
Reread the solution every day this week
Note what you missed, then re-solve it from scratch in a few days and again a week later
Memorize the solution code line by line
check.explanation: Spaced retrieval, re-solving from a blank editor after a gap, is what builds the skill. Rereading mostly builds recognition, and memorized code breaks as soon as the problem changes slightly.

keyTerms.definition: A timed coding test scored automatically by hidden test cases, usually the first technical filter.
A 45 to 60 minute technical interview with one engineer, usually in a shared editor.
The final round: several back-to-back interviews, each interviewer scoring independently.
Understand, Match, Plan, Implement, Review, Evaluate: a repeatable problem-solving method.
The simplest correct solution, usually trying every possibility; a baseline to improve on.
An input at the boundary of what is allowed, such as empty input, one element or all duplicates.
Executing code by hand, line by line, while tracking each variable's value.
Gaining one property, such as speed, by giving up another, such as memory or simplicity.
Mixing problems of different types in one session so you practice choosing the method.
A practice interview where someone else picks the problem and plays the interviewer.
Monitoring during an online test, such as screen or webcam recording and flags for pasting or switching tabs.
A step at some large companies where managers who are choosing interns talk with candidates who passed the interviews.
The stated input limits, such as n <= 100,000, which tell you how fast a solution must be.

summary: Internship hiring usually runs: application review, online assessment, recruiter screen, technical phone screen, a final loop, sometimes team matching, then an offer.
In an OA, read the rules, read every problem first, get correct code before fast code, use the constraints to pick a complexity and test edge cases.
Run the same method every time: understand, match, plan, implement, review, evaluate.
Interviewers score problem solving, coding, communication and testing; thinking out loud makes most of that visible.
When stuck, state the brute force, find the repeated work, walk the pattern list and follow hints.
Practice one pattern at a time, re-solve misses on a spaced schedule, then switch to timed mixed sets and mock interviews.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has their first technical phone screen next week what to do from the moment they hear the problem until the interviewer says time is up, and why each step matters.

questions.question: Put the six steps of the problem-solving method in order.
items: Understand: restate the problem, write examples and edge cases
Match: identify which known pattern fits
Plan: describe the approach and its complexity, and get agreement
Implement: write clean code while explaining decisions
Review: trace an example and the edge cases by hand
Evaluate: state time and space complexity and trade-offs
questions.explanation: Understand, Match, Plan, Implement, Review, Evaluate. The first three happen before any code is written, which is where most of the interview is won or lost.

questions.question: In the UMPIRE method, what does the M stand for?
questions.explanation: Match: after you understand the problem, you look for the known pattern it resembles (hash map, two pointers, BFS and so on). It sits between Understand and Plan.

questions.question: A 45-minute technical phone screen. Put the phases in the order they usually happen.
items: Introductions and a little small talk
Hear the problem and ask clarifying questions
Explain an approach and agree on it
Trace the code by hand and discuss complexity
Ask your own questions about the team
questions.explanation: Interviewers usually save the last few minutes for your questions, so plan to finish testing and the complexity discussion before then. Agreeing on the approach before coding is the step candidates most often skip.

questions.question: The interviewer says: "Given a list of numbers and a target, return the indexes of two numbers that add up to the target." What is the best thing to say first?
choices: "I'll use a hash map. Here's the code."
"Is the optimal solution O(n)?"
"Can there be negatives or duplicates, can I use one element twice, and is there always exactly one answer?"
"Would you like me to write it in Java or Python?"
questions.explanation: Clarifying the input and the expected output comes first, because the answers change the solution (duplicates, reusing an element, what to return when there is no pair). Jumping to code skips Understand and Plan, and asking for the optimal complexity hands the problem solving to the interviewer.

questions.question: You propose a nested-loop solution and the interviewer says, "That works. Can we do better?" What should you do?
choices: Defend the nested loops, since they are correct
Start rewriting with a different data structure without explaining why
Name the bottleneck (the inner loop rescans the list) and look for a way to avoid repeating that work
Ask the interviewer to tell you the optimal approach
questions.explanation: Optimizing starts with finding the repeated work. Saying "the inner loop rescans the list for every element" points straight at the fix (remember what you have seen). Defending correct but slow code ignores the question, and asking for the answer gives away the part being scored.

questions.question: You are planning a two-pointer solution. The interviewer asks, "What if you stored the values you've already seen?" What is the best response?
choices: Repeat the hint in your own words and work out how a hash map of seen values would help
Explain that two pointers is better and keep going
Say "good idea" and keep coding the two-pointer version
Ask whether using their hint will lower your score
questions.explanation: A hint is the interviewer steering you toward a path they know works. Restating it and following it shows you can take input like a good teammate. Brushing it aside, politely or not, is one of the clearest negative signals.

questions.question: You finish coding and the interviewer asks, "How do you know it works?" What is the best response?
choices: "It's the standard solution, so it should be fine."
"Let me trace a small example line by line, then check empty input and duplicates."
"Could you run it for me?"
"I would write unit tests for it later."
questions.explanation: Tracing a normal case and then the edge cases demonstrates verification, one of the four scored areas. Claiming it is standard proves nothing, and deferring testing skips the part they just asked about.

questions.question: Which are useful clarifying questions for "return two numbers in an array that add up to a target"? Choose all that apply.
choices: Can the array contain negative numbers?
Can I use the same element twice?
Is there always exactly one valid answer?
What should I return if no pair exists?
What is the time complexity of the best solution?
Is it okay if I skip the edge cases?
questions.explanation: The first four pin down the input and the output, and each can change the solution. Asking for the best complexity asks the interviewer to solve it for you, and asking to skip edge cases signals you don't plan to verify your work.

questions.question: Match each problem to the pattern to try first.

pairs.left: Find a target in a sorted array
The k largest values in a stream
Fewest moves through a grid maze
Number of ways to climb n stairs

questions.explanation: Sorted plus target suggests binary search. Contiguous range with a condition suggests a sliding window. Top k suggests a heap. Fewest steps in an unweighted grid suggests BFS. Nesting and matching suggest a stack. Counting ways with overlapping subproblems suggests DP.

questions.question: What four areas do most coding-interview rubrics score?
questions.answer: Problem solving (finding and improving an approach), coding (correct, readable code), communication (explaining your reasoning and asking good questions) and testing or verification (checking your own code and edge cases).
questions.explanation: Thinking out loud is what makes problem solving, communication and testing visible. Correct code on its own covers only one of the four.

questions.question: Which narration gives the interviewer the most useful information?
choices: "Now I'm writing a for loop from zero to n."
"Hmm. Hmm. OK."
"I'll keep a set of values I've seen, so checking for a duplicate is O(1) instead of rescanning."
"I'm basically done; I'll explain everything at the end."
questions.explanation: Good narration explains decisions and reasons: what you are doing and why it is efficient. Describing keystrokes adds nothing the interviewer can't see, and saving the explanation for the end leaves them guessing for 20 minutes.

questions.question: How is a typical online assessment graded?
choices: A panel of engineers reads every line
The recruiter reads your comments
Only on whether the code compiles
Hidden test cases run automatically against your code
questions.explanation: OAs run your code against test cases, many of them hidden, and score how many pass. That is why edge cases and constraints matter so much there. Compiling is only the first hurdle.

questions.question: How does a technical phone screen usually differ from an online assessment?
choices: It is graded only by hidden tests
It covers only behavioral questions
It is always a take-home project
An engineer watches you work, and your explanation and hand testing count, often without running the code
questions.explanation: In a phone screen a person evaluates how you reach the solution, not just the final code. Many shared editors don't run code, so tracing by hand and explaining your reasoning carry a lot of weight.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of has_pair? Use Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: When no pair exists, the inner loop runs n-1, then n-2, down to 0 times: about n^2/2 checks in total. Constants drop, so it is O(n^2). The early return only helps when a pair is found quickly.

questions.question: What is the worst-case extra space complexity of has_duplicate? Use Big-O notation.
questions.explanation: When there are no duplicates, every element is added to seen, so the set grows to n items. Time is O(n) on average, because each membership test and add on a set is O(1) on average.

questions.question: Which test case exposes a bug in average?
choices: average([2, 4, 6])
average([-1, 1])
average([])
average([5])
questions.explanation: An empty list makes len(nums) zero, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError. Ask the interviewer what an empty list should return (None, 0 or an error) and handle it. [-1, 1] returns 0.0, which is correct.

questions.question: Tracing max_window_sum([1, 2, 3, 10], 2) by hand gives 5, but the answer should be 13 (from 3 + 10). What is wrong?
questions.code:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    """Largest sum of any k consecutive numbers."""
    window = sum(nums[:k])
    best = window
    for i in range(k, len(nums) - 1):
        window += nums[i] - nums[i - k]
        best = max(best, window)
    return best
choices: The first window should be sum(nums[:k + 1])
The loop stops one index early, so the last window is never checked
The window should subtract nums[i - k + 1] instead of nums[i - k]
best should start at 0 instead of the first window
questions.explanation: range(k, len(nums) - 1) skips i = len(nums) - 1, the step that slides the window onto the last element. It should be range(k, len(nums)). Subtracting nums[i - k] is correct: when the window gains nums[i], the element that falls out is k positions back.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the first pass counts each character correctly.
choices: None
ch
questions.explanation: get returns the default when the key is missing, so the first time a character appears its count becomes 0 + 1 = 1. A default of 1 would start every count at 2, and None + 1 raises a TypeError.

questions.question: What are the time and space complexity of the two-pass first_unique_char solution (count, then scan)?
choices: O(n^2) time, because there are two loops
O(n log n) time and O(n) space
O(n) time and O(k) space, where k is the number of distinct characters
O(2n) time, which is slower than O(n)
questions.explanation: Two loops one after the other cost O(n) + O(n) = O(n); only nested loops multiply. The dict holds one entry per distinct character, so space is O(k), which is O(1) if the alphabet is fixed (for example 26 lowercase letters). O(2n) is just O(n).

questions.question: You solved "does this list contain a duplicate?" with a hash set. The interviewer says: "Memory is very tight, and you may modify the list." What is the best adjustment?
choices: Keep the hash set, because O(n) time is always the priority
Sort the list in place and compare neighbors: O(n log n) time with little extra memory
Use nested loops, because O(n^2) time is the only way to get O(1) space
Store the values in a dict instead of a set
questions.explanation: After an in-place sort, duplicates sit next to each other, so one scan finds them. You trade some time (O(n log n) instead of O(n)) for memory. Nested loops also use O(1) space, but they are not the only option once sorting in place is allowed, and they are much slower. A dict uses as much memory as a set.

questions.question: Ten minutes remain. You have a correct brute-force idea but no faster one, and the interviewer hasn't offered a hint. What is the best move?
choices: Keep thinking silently about the optimal solution
Ask to skip to a different problem
Write partial code for a half-formed faster idea
Say you'll implement the brute force now, code it cleanly, and explain where you would optimize
questions.explanation: Working, readable code plus a clear explanation of the next optimization shows coding, communication and problem solving. Silence earns nothing, and half-finished code for an idea you can't complete usually scores lower than a clean brute force.

questions.question: Which behaviors usually hurt a candidate's score? Choose all that apply.
choices: Long unexplained silences
Starting to code before agreeing on an approach
Arguing with a hint instead of exploring it
Announcing a short pause to think
Asking whether the input can be empty
questions.explanation: Silence hides your reasoning, coding before agreeing risks building the wrong thing, and fighting hints signals you are hard to work with. A short announced pause and clarifying questions about edge cases are both good habits.

questions.question: You needed the solution to finish a practice problem. What should you do so the lesson actually sticks?
questions.answer: Write down what you missed (the signal or the step), then re-solve the problem from a blank editor a few days later and again about a week after that. Spaced re-solving builds the skill; rereading only builds recognition.
questions.explanation: Retrieval after a delay is what makes memory durable. Logging the miss turns a vague "I didn't get it" into a specific signal you can watch for next time.

questions.question: Why switch to mixed problem sets after you have learned several patterns one at a time?
choices: Real interviews don't tell you the pattern, so you need practice choosing it
Mixed sets are easier, which builds confidence
Mixing lets you skip the patterns you find hard
It reduces the total number of problems you need to review
questions.explanation: Practicing one pattern at a time teaches the technique, but you always know which tool to use. Interleaving forces you to recognize the signals and pick the tool, which is exactly what an interview demands.

questions.question: The interviewer asks, "Is your hash map solution really O(n)?" Which answer is most accurate?
choices: Yes, because hash map operations are always O(1)
No, hash maps are O(log n) per operation, so it is O(n log n)
On average yes, since each insert and lookup is O(1) on average; heavy collisions can make lookups O(n), so the worst case is O(n^2), which a good hash function makes very unlikely
It depends only on how much memory the computer has
questions.explanation: Hash tables give O(1) expected time per operation, not guaranteed O(1). Naming the average case and the rare worst case shows you understand the structure. O(log n) per operation describes tree-based maps such as Java's TreeMap, not hash maps.

questions.question: In a four-interview final loop, your second interview goes badly. What should you do?
choices: Tell the next interviewer it went badly so they can adjust
Ask the recruiter to end the loop early
Spend part of the next interview revisiting the earlier problem
Reset and treat the next interview fresh, since each interviewer usually scores independently and the decision looks at the whole loop
questions.explanation: Interviewers in a loop typically write their feedback separately, and one weaker round does not automatically sink you. Carrying the last round into the next one is what turns one bad interview into two.

questions.question: Which set of tests gives the best coverage for a function that returns the smallest number in a list?
questions.explanation: Good tests vary along the dimensions that break code: empty, one element, all equal, negatives and zero, and the minimum in different positions. The other sets repeat the same shape of input, so they would all pass or fail together.

questions.question: You traced your binary search on [1, 3, 5, 7] with target 7 and it worked. Which extra cases are most likely to reveal an off-by-one bug?
choices: Target 3 in [1, 3, 5, 7]
Target 5 in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
A target that is missing (such as 4) and a one-element list
Target 7 in [1, 3, 5, 7] again, with clearer variable names
questions.explanation: Off-by-one bugs in binary search show up when the loop must end without finding anything (the low and high bounds cross) or when the range is tiny. More found-target cases in the middle of normal arrays exercise the path that already works.

questions.question: Your function answers "does this list contain value x?" by scanning the list. The interviewer says it will be called a million times on the same list with different x. What do you propose?
choices: Build a set from the list once, then answer each query in O(1) on average
Keep scanning, since each scan is only O(n)
Sort the list before every query, then binary search
Cache only the last answer in a variable
questions.explanation: Paying O(n) once to build a set makes every later query O(1) on average, so a million queries cost about n + 1,000,000 operations instead of a million times n. Sorting once and binary searching would also work, but sorting before every query is worse than scanning.

questions.question: While you learn a new pattern each week, what does a short daily Recurse review do for you?
choices: Replaces the need to solve problems
Brings back earlier patterns' signals and complexities right before you would forget them
Teaches new patterns you have not studied yet
Lets you skip mock interviews
questions.explanation: Spaced repetition schedules each card for just before you are likely to forget it, so week-one patterns are still sharp in week eight. It supports problem solving and mock interviews; it does not replace them.

questions.question: You open an OA with three problems and 90 minutes. What should you do first?
choices: Read all three problems and their constraints, then start with the one you are surest of
Start coding problem 1 immediately
Search the web for each problem title
Write long comments explaining your plan for the grader
questions.explanation: A minute per problem to read and note constraints lets you start with the one you are surest of and plan your time. Diving into problem 1 blindly can burn the whole test on the hardest problem.

questions.question: The constraints say 1 <= n <= 100,000. Which time complexity should your solution aim for?
choices: O(n^2) is fine for any OA
O(n log n) or better
O(n^3), if the code is short
questions.explanation: With n = 100,000, O(n^2) is about 10^10 steps and will usually time out, while O(n log n) is under 2 million steps. Constraints are a hint about the intended solution.

questions.question: Which actions can get an online assessment flagged or disqualified when the rules do not allow them? Choose all that apply.
choices: Asking an AI assistant to write the solution
Having a friend help over a call
Pasting code from a solutions website
Running your code with the platform's Run button
Writing a helper function
questions.explanation: Outside help from an AI assistant, another person or a solutions site is what proctoring and similarity checks look for. Using the platform's own Run button and writing helper functions are normal parts of solving the problem.

questions.question: Your OA solution passes the samples but fails two hidden tests, and 15 minutes remain. What should you check first?
choices: Edge cases such as empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives and the largest allowed size
Variable names, because graders read them
Rewriting the whole solution in another language
Nothing; hidden tests are random
questions.explanation: Hidden tests are mostly edge cases and large inputs. Checking empty input, one element, duplicates, negatives and the maximum size finds most failures quickly. Rewriting from scratch with 15 minutes left rarely pays off.

questions.question: A problem allows n up to 20. About how many subsets does a brute-force search over all subsets check? Give the exact number.
questions.explanation: 2^20 = 1,048,576, about a million, which is quick. Tiny limits like n <= 20 often signal that trying every subset (backtracking or bitmasks) is the intended approach.

questions.question: Match each stage of the process to what it mainly checks.

pairs.right: Correct code that passes hidden tests in time
Solving one or two problems while explaining
Several independent technical and behavioral interviews

questions.explanation: Each stage filters for something different: the OA for correct code under time pressure, the recruiter screen for fit and logistics, the phone screen for solving while explaining, and the final loop for all of it plus behavioral evidence.

questions.question: After passing a final loop at a large company, you are invited to "team matching" calls with two managers. How should you treat them?
choices: As a formality, since the offer is already guaranteed
As short two-way interviews: share your interests and ask about their team's work
As another coding round, so practice hard problems only
As a chance to negotiate pay with the manager
questions.explanation: Managers are deciding whether you fit their team, and you are deciding whether you want to join it. Prepare a short pitch and specific questions about their work. They are lighter than technical rounds, but not a formality.

questions.question: Your video interview is tomorrow morning. Which preparation helps most tonight?
choices: Learning three new advanced algorithms until 2 a.m.
Reading the company's entire engineering blog
Nothing; preparation makes you nervous
Testing the link, camera, microphone and connection, reviewing your notes and stories, and sleeping well
questions.explanation: Removing technical risk and arriving rested protects everything you have practiced. Cramming new hard problems the night before adds stress without adding much skill.

questions.question: What should you do right after each real interview?
questions.answer: Write down every problem and question while it is fresh, what went well and what did not, add the misses to your practice log to re-solve, and send a short thank-you note to the recruiter.
questions.explanation: Interview notes are the most valuable practice material you will get, and memory fades within hours. The misses become problems to re-solve and cards to review.

questions.question: An OA problem reads input from standard input instead of giving you a function signature. What is the best preparation?
choices: Nothing; input parsing is always done for you
Practice reading input in that style (for example with input() or sys.stdin in Python) on the platform's practice test beforehand
Hard-code the sample input into your solution
Ask the proctor to convert it to a function
questions.explanation: Input handling is a common, avoidable way to lose time. Practicing on the platform's sample test means you already know how to read lines and parse numbers when the clock is running.

questions.question: Halfway through a 90-minute OA, problem 2 still passes zero tests and problem 3 is unread. What is the best move?
choices: Keep going on problem 2 until it works, however long it takes
Restart the assessment
Leave problem 2 blank and stop the test early
Submit what you have for problem 2, move to problem 3, and come back if time remains
questions.explanation: Problems usually score separately, so partial credit on problem 3 is often worth more than more time sunk into problem 2. Submitting what you have keeps any credit it earns, and you can return if time remains.
